Analyst Mindset

L1 detects, documents, escalates

The first tier isn’t where incidents get solved — it’s where they get caught. My rule, learned from lab work and Security+ study alike: an analyst who guesses is a liability; an analyst who documents is a force multiplier.

I don’t remediate beyond my authority and I don’t sit on a maybe. If traffic looks like a scan, I capture the pattern, the source, the targets, and the timestamps — then it goes up the chain as a ticket someone senior can act on in minutes, not a mystery they have to re-investigate.

Lab · Network ReconStatus: Ongoing

Home Network Recon Lab

A Kali Linux VM in bridged mode, dropped onto my real home LAN — a T-Mobile 5G gateway (192.168.12.1) plus a mesh access point — so every scan hits real devices, real services, and real noise instead of a sterile sandbox.

  • Host discovery: netdiscover sweeps to inventory everything on the subnet — phones, hosts, IoT — and track what joins or leaves.
  • Enumeration: Nmap service and port sweeps with banner grabbing to fingerprint what each device actually exposes.
  • Attack simulation: ARP-spoof blackholing experiments to watch traffic die — and to learn exactly which telemetry betrays it.
  • Known limit, stated plainly: Wi-Fi deauth work needs a USB adapter with monitor mode — theory understood, hardware on the list.

What it demonstrates: recon methodology from the defender’s seat — inventory first, enumerate second, and knowing exactly which telemetry an attack leaves behind.

Skill Drill · Traffic AnalysisStatus: Ongoing

Reading Packets Like an Analyst

Structured Wireshark practice built around one question: given a capture, what is this host actually doing — and should anyone care?

  • Handshake fluency: SYN → SYN-ACK → ACK means open; a RST-ACK answer means closed. No guessing, just flags.
  • Scan fingerprints: a completed handshake torn down by the scanner’s own RST is the signature of a TCP connect scan.
  • Beaconing radar: outbound connections to port 4444 on a steady 60-second rhythm pattern-match Metasploit-style C2; the same rhythm to 443 earns a second look, not a siren.
  • Port literacy: a working mental map of common services, so an odd port in a log line reads as a sentence, not a number.

What it demonstrates: verdict discipline — separating a real C2 pattern from benign look-alikes using flags, ports, and timing instead of gut feel.

Build · Python AutomationStatus: Working on my PC

“Hey Yami” — On-Device Voice Assistant

A fully hands-free voice front-end for my desktop, built after a commercial wake-word service rejected my signup. Everything runs on-device — no cloud accounts, no subscriptions. It turned into the best detection-engineering lesson of my year: building a detector is easy; tuning one that doesn’t cry wolf is the job.

[wake] vosk grammar match "hey yummy" (dictionary soundalike for “hey yami”)
[wake] openWakeWord custom model — true-phrase upgrade, training in Colab
[hear] faster-whisper (base, int8) transcription → request delivered to app
[tune] false trigger: room audio fired the listener → fix: fire on FINAL results only, never partials
  • Pipeline: Vosk wake-word grammar → spoken greeting (pyttsx3) → speech capture with Vosk-based endpointing — the recorder uses the same “ears” as the wake stage after a loudness gate proved unreliable → faster-whisper transcription → automated delivery into the target app.
  • False-positive war: an early build fired on TV audio and delivered garbled “requests.” Fixes shipped: final-result-only triggering, focus-first window reuse, and a status overlay so the detector’s state is always visible. Exactly the triage loop: detect, verify, tune, document.
  • Zero-training fallback: a Vosk-only edition that works tonight with no model training, documented alongside the openWakeWord edition.

What it demonstrates: detection tuning — a detector that cries wolf is a design flaw you iterate on: observe the false positives, tighten the trigger, document, retest.
